DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
## Summary of the review

The paper proposes three main-course price rises from 1 April:
- fish and chips to £17.50;
- the burger to £16.00;
- sirloin steak to £28.00.

It also proposes replacing the mushroom risotto with a vegetarian special. It projects £810 a week (£42,120 a year) in extra gross profit, lifting the main-course margin to about 71%. Its case is that all three prices stay below the competitor midpoint and that the customer base is loyal.

## Verdict

The price rises are reasonable and the competitor check supports them. But the paper's own data contradict the risotto proposal: the risotto has the **highest** margin on the menu, not the weakest. The profit projection also leaves out the 12% beef price rise that Section 4 itself reports, and probably VAT as well. Once those are included, the real gain is substantially smaller than £42,000.

## 1. The risotto is the most profitable dish by margin

Table 1 gives the risotto an **80% margin**, the highest on the menu. Its gross profit per plate is £11.20, more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90). The dish with the weakest margin is the **sirloin steak at 60%**, which the paper keeps, rightly, since it earns £15.60 a plate.

The risotto's sales of 90 a week are the joint lowest, tied with specials. But replacing it with a seasonal special at the same price will probably *lower* margin, since specials currently run at 64%. On the paper's own figures, the risotto is earning its place. It is also likely the dish that settles where groups with a vegetarian in them choose to eat. If there's a reason to replace it, such as staff time or wastage, the paper should say so; the margin argument points the other way.

## 2. The projection leaves out the beef price rise

Section 4 says beef rises **12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices take effect. Section 5.3 assumes costs are unchanged. Applying the rise:

| Dish | Price rise | Extra cost per plate (if all of the cost is beef) | Net gain per plate | Plates/week | Weekly gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £1.00 | £0 | £1.00 | 310 | £310 |
| Burger | £1.00 | up to £0.50 | ≥ £0.50 | 260 | ≥ £130 |
| Steak | £2.00 | up to £1.25 | ≥ £0.75 | 120 | ≥ £90 |
| **Total** | | | | | **≈ £530–£570** |

The lower figure assumes the whole plate cost is beef; the upper allows for chips, buns and garnishes. That is roughly **£28,000–£30,000 a year, not £42,000**. The steak's margin actually *falls* even after its £2 rise: £28.00 price against an £11.65 cost is about 58%.

The 71% margin claim has the same problem. Excluding specials, the current main-course margin works out at about 69.9%. With the price rises and *unchanged* costs it would reach about 71.3%, which matches the paper. With the beef rise included, it stays at about **69.7%, roughly where it is now**.

## 3. VAT probably reduces the gain further

The margins in Table 1 are calculated on menu prices. In a UK restaurant, those include 20% VAT, so only five-sixths of each price rise is actually kept: £1.00 on the menu is about £0.83 to the business. If Table 1 uses VAT-inclusive prices:
- the true margins are lower than shown, e.g. fish and chips is about 63%, not 69%;
- the gain after beef costs falls to roughly **£400 a week, or about £20,000 a year**.

Check with whoever does the accounts which basis the 67% and 70% targets use, and make the paper consistent.

## 4. "Remain the value option" isn't quite right

The prices do stay below the competitor midpoint for every dish:
- fish and chips: £17.50 against a midpoint of £17.98;
- burger: £16.00 against £16.50;
- steak: £28.00 against £29.50.

But the paper also says The Copper Kettle is currently **the cheapest** on all three dishes. After the rises it won't be on any of them: £16.95, £15.50 and £27.00 are each lower. That may be fine, but it's a real change in position, and it's worth stating plainly.

The 60% repeat base cuts both ways. Loyal guests are more forgiving, but they're also the ones who know the old prices and will notice the increases.

## 5. Monitoring against January–February will be misleading

January and February are usually the quietest months of the year. Volumes in April and May will probably rise anyway, which could hide a drop caused by the price rises. Compare instead with the **same weeks last year**, adjusted for overall cover numbers. Tracking each dish's share of main-course sales would also help.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. Section 8 says "six trading days a week".
- **Where the margin has slipped.** The main-course margin is already near 70%, yet overall food margin is 67%. The slippage may be partly in starters, desserts or specials. Those are outside this review, but worth checking before treating main-course prices as the whole answer.
- **The curry.** It wasn't included in the competitor check. Its price may be worth reviewing too.

## 7. What is sound

- **The basic arithmetic is correct.** The table margins, the £810 total (£310 + £260 + £240) and £42,120 a year all check out.
- **The competitor check is useful**, and every "below midpoint" claim is accurate.
- **The price rises are modest.** The last change was in September 2024, so a rise is reasonable.
- **The paper reports the beef notice.** The information needed for an accurate projection is there; it just isn't applied.
- **Weekly monitoring by dish** is the right approach; only the baseline needs changing.

## 8. The author's description vs. the document

- **"The mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu."** It has the highest (80%).
- **"£810 a week or about £42,000 a year."** This leaves out the beef rise the paper itself reports, and probably VAT.
- **"Lifts our main-course margin to about 71%."** With beef included, the margin stays at about 70%.
- **"We remain the value option."** The restaurant moves from cheapest to mid-range on all three dishes.

## Recommendations

1. Keep the risotto, or give a reason other than margin for replacing it.
2. Recalculate the projection with the 12% beef rise, using the actual beef share of each plate's cost.
3. Confirm whether margins are calculated before or after VAT, and restate the figures on that basis.
4. Describe the new pricing position accurately: below the competitor midpoint, no longer the cheapest.
5. Monitor against the same weeks last year, not January–February.
6. Fix "six trading days".

With these changes, the price rises are still worth making. The owners just need to know the realistic gain is probably in the range of £20,000–£30,000 a year rather than £42,000.

I can redraft Section 5 with the corrected projection, or set up a simple sheet that recalculates margins before and after VAT for each dish.
